The yolk-sac larva of Blue catfish (Ictalurus furcatus JR) emerges after a period of approximately 6 to 9 days [ab = approximately 6 to 9 days] when eggs are incubated at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], a duration that reflects the species' relatively rapid embryonic development among large-bodied ictalurids. At the moment of eclosion, the prolarvae are notably small, with a fork length at birth of approximately 1.4 centimeters [Lb = approximately 1.4 centimeters], a size that aligns closely with field observations reporting total lengths between 16 and 17.6 millimeters for newly hatched individuals in the James River system. The endotrophic phase, during which the larva relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves, constitutes the first portion of this age interval. The transition to exogenous feeding, marked by mouth opening and the onset of active prey capture, follows yolk-sac resorption. This developmental schedule was determined under controlled laboratory conditions mimicking the thermal regime of natal habitats, where consistent water temperatures around 27 °C are typical during the spawning season. Such a relatively abbreviated pre-feeding interval is ecologically significant because it minimizes the window of vulnerability to starvation during the critical shift from lecithotrophy to planktivory, a period that can be particularly hazardous for pelagic teleost larvae.

Sexual maturation in Blue catfish from the James River population occurs at a remarkably small body size compared to the species' ultimate growth potential. Examination of gonad condition in field-collected specimens revealed that the smallest mature individual, a male, measured 31.5 centimeters [Lp = 31.5 centimeters] in fork length, while the mean fork length at puberty across all sampled fish was somewhat larger at 34.3 centimeters. The corresponding somatic wet weight at puberty for the smallest mature fish was recorded as 398 grams [Wwp = 398 grams], a value that highlights the substantial energetic investment required to reach reproductive competence. Under the thermal conditions typical of temperate lotic habitats where this species resides, specifically at an average water temperature of 17.3 °C [T = 17.3 °C], the time since birth at puberty is estimated at approximately 7 years [tp = approximately 7 years]. This protracted juvenile period, spanning several years of growth before the onset of gonadal recrudescence, is characteristic of iteroparous freshwater teleosts that prioritize somatic accumulation prior to first spawning. The age at first reproduction, which typically follows soon after puberty, is similarly delayed.

Substantial sexual dimorphism in ultimate body size is evident within this species, with males attaining a greater asymptotic fork length than females. Analysis of maximal size records indicates that females reach an ultimate fork length of 105.5 centimeters [Li = 105.5 centimeters], whereas males achieve a slightly larger ultimate fork length of 110.2 centimeters [Li = 110.2 centimeters]. This pattern of male-biased size dimorphism is relatively uncommon among ictalurids and may reflect differential selective pressures acting on the sexes, possibly related to male-male competition for spawning sites or nest-guarding territories. The corresponding ultimate somatic wet weights further underscore this disparity: females attain a maximum somatic wet weight of 25,725 grams [Wwi = 25,725 grams], while males achieve a considerably greater ultimate somatic wet weight of 29,630 grams [Wwi = 29,630 grams]. It is worth noting that some online sources, such as Wikipedia entries accessed in early 2020, report much higher total body masses of up to 64,864 grams, but those figures likely include large, unsexed individuals or may reflect populations with significantly different growth trajectories and environmental conditions.

Reproductive output in large female Blue catfish is substantial, reflecting the strong relationship between somatic mass and gamete production. At 25,725 grams [Wwi = 25,725 grams]—the benchmark adult female mass for this population—the extrapolated maximum reproductive rate under the prevailing thermal regime of 17.3 °C [T = 17.3 °C] corresponds to a daily egg production of approximately 328 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 328 eggs per day] when spawning is active. This fecundity estimate is derived from the observed proportionality between body mass and clutch size in ictalurids. The dry mass of individual eggs, measured as the mean egg dry weight for the James River stock, is remarkably small at 0.007093 grams , a value consistent with the production of large numbers of relatively yolk-poor ova typical of broadcast-spawning teleosts. In comparative terms, the ratio of egg dry mass to female body mass is exceedingly low, suggesting an r-selected reproductive strategy in which high fecundity compensates for low per-offspring investment. The breeding individuals, which are gravid during the spawning season, release demersal adhesive eggs that adhere to submerged structures in the turbid riverine environment.

Longevity in Blue catfish shows pronounced variation between the sexes, with females generally outliving males under natural conditions. Based on the oldest documented individuals in the James River system, which were assessed using otolith annuli analysis, the maximum lifespan for females is approximately 25 years [am = approximately 25 years] when maintained at the mean annual water temperature of 17.3 °C [T = 17.3 °C]. In contrast, male maximum lifespan is considerably shorter, estimated at around 20 years [am = around 20 years] under identical thermal conditions, a difference that may reflect higher metabolic costs associated with male territoriality and nest defense during the spawning season. at a temperature of 17.3 °C [T = 17.3 °C]The literature occasionally reports extreme longevities of up to 34 years regardless of sex, but such records are exceptional and likely originate from populations in deep, thermally stable reservoirs. This sex-specific disparity in lifespan is not uncommon among iteroparous freshwater fishes with size-dimorphic growth patterns, and it aligns with the broader observation that the sex investing more heavily in reproductive behavior often experiences accelerated senescence. The progressive deterioration of physiological function in senescent adults ultimately leads to natural mortality once the lifespan has been completed.
